title: A hot-dry summer increased the next-year growth of bark beetle tree-mortality area by about 23% per standard deviation in western US aerial surveys, 1999-2025
abstract: Question: do hot and dry years increase the next-year growth of tree-mortality area from bark beetles in western US forests when survey effort, outbreak size and host depletion are controlled? Approach: we wrote the plan before we related the data to climate. We put USDA Forest Service aerial-survey (IDS) maps of 1997-2025 for all six western regions on 0.5-degree cells. A hot-drought index (HD) combines summer Tmax and water-year precipitation from NOAA CPC data. The model compares log growth of mapped mortality from survey year t to t+1 with HD in summer t, with cell and region-by-year effects, and uses only cells that the survey covered by at least 25% in both years. Intervals come from a bootstrap over survey years. Result: for drought-associated bark beetles (western pine beetle, fir engraver, Douglas-fir beetle, ips and others, pooled), 1 SD of HD increased log growth by +0.206 (95% interval +0.090 to +0.302), about 23% per SD, in 8,906 cell-year pairs. The estimate was positive in all six regions (intervals excluded zero in two) and in 1999-2011 and 2012-2024, and a placebo (HD two summers later) gave +0.005. All pre-declared criteria were met. Dryness carried the signal (+0.133) and heat added to it mainly in dry years (hot x dry +0.127); heat alone was uncertain. Mountain pine beetle (+0.077) and spruce beetle (+0.006) did not respond clearly, and defoliators tended to decrease (-0.204). Drought did not change survey coverage. In a forward test (fit 1999-2011, predict 2012-2024) the drought terms reduced error by 22% with region trends, but a negative control also gained 13%; without trends the gain was 8% (1% to 15%) and the control gained none. Limitations: mapped polygons are not tree counts; the design uses within-region contrasts and removes region-wide drought years; 0.5-degree climate is coarse; 1999-2011 alone is uncertain; the survey method changed in 2015-2017. We also report that the shared campaign IDS copies are truncated and that DMSM-era defoliation uses new damage codes.

citations.reason: Same IDS gridding and fixed-effects design (mountain pine beetle and winter cold, null); we extend it to summer drought, other bark beetle agents and Regions 3 and 5.
Review of drought impacts on US forest insects; our within-region test supports the drought-bark beetle link for drought-associated agents.
Reported drought-induced spruce beetle outbreaks; our spruce beetle estimate was near zero at 0.5-degree scale.
